The Blue-necked tanager Stilpnia cyanicollis is a colorful passerine of the Andean cloud forests whose life-history traits remain relatively poorly documented compared to many lowland thraupids. Field data from the Cordillera Oriental of Colombia indicate that eggs, when incubated at 34 °C [T = 34 °C], produce altricial nestlings following a brief developmental period of about 13.5 days [ab = about 13.5 days]. This incubation duration is modest relative to the protracted embryonic development seen in some high-altitude congeners, likely reflecting the moderate thermal conditions of the nest microhabitat. Shortly after hatching, the altricial young are entirely dependent on biparental provisioning, with both parents delivering arthropod prey to the nestlings throughout the day. The chick growth trajectory during this early phase is characterized by rapid mass accumulation, setting the stage for the subsequent milestones of feather development and eventual fledging. Studies of captive individuals have confirmed that the gestational physiology of the egg stage is tightly coupled with ambient nest temperature, underscoring the role of thermal regulation in shaping early ontogenetic schedules.

Under typical active-season thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the fledging event is recorded approximately 15.5 days after hatching [tx = approximately 15.5 days after hatching], marking the point at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and departs from the nest. This relatively short nestling period is characteristic of many tropical passerines, where predation pressure on the nest is high and rapid development confers a selective advantage. Once the fledgling leaves the nest, it enters a phase of post-fledging dependence during which parental feeding continues for several additional weeks while the young bird refines its foraging skills. The attainment of full flight feather maturation is a gradual process, and survivorship during this vulnerable interval is influenced by food availability and habitat structure. Comparative data from related thraupid species suggest that the fledging age of this species is near the lower end of the family range, consistent with its life-history strategy of minimizing nest exposure time.

Sexual maturation in the Blue-necked tanager is reached approximately 46.5 days after hatching [tp = approximately 46.5 days after hatching] when maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a developmental timeline that reflects the relatively rapid pace of gonadal development in this species. At this point, the juvenile bird undergoes the transition from the subadult plumage to the definitive adult coloration, a process that is mediated by hormonal changes associated with the onset of gametogenesis. The timing of puberty appears to be influenced by nutritional condition, as individuals in high-quality habitats with abundant fruit resources tend to achieve maturity at slightly younger ages. The age at first successful reproduction, however, is delayed further beyond the onset of sexual maturity. Under the same thermal regimen of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the first brood is initiated at approximately 438 days after hatching [tR = approximately 438 days after hatching], indicating a substantial lag between physiological readiness and actual breeding effort. This delay may be linked to territory acquisition and the establishment of a stable pair bond.

Reproductive output in Stilpnia cyanicollis is modest, with females producing two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch] and typically raising a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This low annual reproductive investment is characteristic of many Neotropical passerines, which trade off high per-nestling provisioning effort for reduced brood size compared to their temperate counterparts. The annual reproductive rate is approximately two eggs per year [Ri = approximately two eggs per year]. The hatchlings themselves are extremely altricial, weighing only 2.86 grams [Ww0 = 2.86 grams] at emergence, a mass that represents a minuscule fraction of the adult female body weight. The yolk reserves are rapidly depleted during the first few days, after which the nestlings rely entirely on the protein-rich diet supplied by the attending adults. Growth rates during the nestling period are steep, with body mass increasing several-fold before fledging occurs. The maximum recorded longevity for this species is approximately 8.6 years [am = approximately 8.6 years] under field conditions at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a lifespan that is typical for a small-bodied tanager inhabiting relatively stable tropical environments.

Adult females of the Blue-necked tanager attain a maximum body mass of 17 grams [Wwi = 17 grams], placing the species among the smaller members of the genus Stilpnia. This modest size is associated with a high mass-specific metabolic demand, and respirometry measurements have quantified the basal metabolic rate at 63.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 63.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The elevated metabolic rate likely reflects the energetic costs of maintaining body temperature in the cool, humid environment of the cloud forest, where ambient temperatures often fall well below the thermoneutral zone of the species. Foraging behavior is correspondingly intense, with adults making frequent trips to fruiting trees and epiphytes to sustain both their own energy balance and that of their offspring. The species' life-history strategy appears to be shaped by a trade-off between high daily energy expenditure and a relatively extended lifespan, consistent with the pace-of-life syndrome observed in many tropical resident birds. Understanding these physiological constraints is essential for predicting how the species may respond to ongoing habitat fragmentation and climate change in the Andean highlands.
